newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG prime minister orders curfew to fight crime.
newsitem.headline: PNG prime minister orders curfew to fight crime.

text.p: A two-month nationwide curfew will be imposed in Papua New Guinea starting on Friday in an attempt to combat a wave of violent crime sweeping the South Pacific nation, Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan announced.
Police in the Papua New Guinea capital Port Moresby were given "shoot to kill" orders last month after a surge of violence by armed gangs, known as "rascals", in the city.

The nightly curfew will be imposed between 9.00 p.m. and 5.00 a.m. and special "daylight curfews" will be imposed in areas police regard as criminal hide-outs, Chan said in a statement issued on Tuesday night.
The government also decided to allocate an extra 1.7 million kina (US$1.2 million) to police to implement and run the curfew, Chan said.

Chan said the curfew was originally planned for early next year to coincide with preparations for elections, but had been brought forward because of the recent spate of violent crimes in Port Moresby.
"The police will be adequately armed in their duties and the government will back the operations in full," Chan said.
"If you doubt me, you've got something coming. We will go forward until the criminals are behind bars," he said.
"Police will trade fire with fire and catch the hooligans and scoundrels and lock them up."
Port Moresby is known as one of the world's most dangerous cities. Rising unemployment and urban drift has led to the growth of criminal gangs in recent years.
Large parts of the city centre are no-go areas for tourists and foreign residents, who live in houses surrounded by high walls and razor wire.

In the past few weeks police and gangs have traded gun fire in street shoot-outs in Port Moresby, banks have been robbed, and a "pay-back" murder left four school boys and one man dead on a beach in the capital.
Chan said Port Moresby, Lae and Mount Hagen were the three cities known to police as criminal locations.
"Police have declared war on criminals," police commissioner Robert Nenta told reporters. "I am tired of my policemen and women being the sitting ducks," Nenta said.
"We are aware of what the criminals have in the way of firepower, what they are planning and I will ensure that our police will be provided with better weapons," he said.
Gangs are normally armed with high-powered rifles, handguns and machetes, although police last week recovered a stolen defence force grenade launcher after a shoot-out with a gang.
Speaking at a conference on security in Port Moresby last month, Chan said law and order was now a focus of national security.
"Of all the menaces to our stability the most troubling is urban jobless growth, exacerbated by unplanned and excessive urban drift," Chan said.
"Internal disorder and unrest, extreme social dissatisfaction, can be a potent invitation for malicious forces," he said.
